summary: Meyer's reply to RFC 467, describing the lost allocation and half-closed connection problems of the Host-Host protocol and offering comments and alternative suggestions on the BBN proposal. It reviews how connections and allocation worked at the time. It updates RFC 467.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 492 responds to proposed fixes for two Host-Host connection problems: stalled data flow and connections left open in one host's records after a failure. Meyer argues that the first problem may signal lost messages and should be detected, not hidden by resetting counters.

questions: what is the lost allocate problem
subtitle: A response to proposed fixes for stalled and half-closed Host-Host connections.

tldr.problem: The Host-Host protocol could leave a connection stalled when allocation messages were lost, or leave one host believing a connection remained open after the other host crashed.
tldr.mechanism: E. Meyer criticizes reset messages proposed in RFC 467 and suggests comparing allocation values after a GVB/RET exchange to detect errors.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a comment on RFC 467 that argues lost messages should be exposed and reported rather than silently masked.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 492's status as Unknown. It updates RFC 467 and is a comment document, not a complete protocol specification.

sections.title: Lost Allocations and Half-Closed Connections
sections.content:
The Host-Host protocol lets a receiving host control data flow by allocating space to the sending host. The sender may send only the amount allowed by that allocation. If an allocation message is lost, the sender may wait for more permission while the receiver waits for data, leaving the connection blocked. A lost data message can produce similar symptoms. The memo calls this the lost allocate phenomenon.

A half-closed connection occurs when one host crashes and loses its connection records while the other host still believes the connection is open. The restarted host may then be unable to reconnect to the same socket because the other host considers it occupied.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver gives the sender permission to send data. If a permission message or data message is lost, each host can wait for the other indefinitely.

sections.title: Why Meyer Objects to RFC 467's Reset Proposal
sections.content:
RFC 467 proposes RCS and RCR control messages to reset allocation counters at both ends of a connection. Meyer argues that this addresses the symptom of a stalled connection rather than the cause. If data messages are also being lost, resetting allocation counters could conceal a missing part of a file and allow the error to appear later as a larger problem.

For half-closed connections, RFC 467 proposes that a host silently close its local connection when later messages reveal an inconsistency. Meyer argues that this can make bugs harder to diagnose, may assume incorrectly that the other NCP closed the connection, and does not cover every case.
sections.plainLanguage: Meyer argues that resetting counters can make a connection move again without revealing that messages were lost. A missing part of a file could then go unnoticed.

sections.title: Compare Allocation Values to Detect Errors
sections.content:
As an interim alternative, Meyer proposes a modified exchange using Give-Back allocation (GVB) and Return Allocation (RET). A receiving host sends GVB with both fraction fields set to all 1s. The sender stops transmitting, waits for the RFNM for its last message so the pipeline is empty, and returns the remaining allocation in RET.

The receiving host compares the returned allocation with its own counters. If they match, it can send a new allocation. If they differ, an error may have occurred; the response is left to the host, but Meyer says the user and a person monitoring network performance should at least be notified. For half-closed connections, he recommends stricter use of RST and lists rules for purging connections to a host reported dead, resetting before communication, and reporting inconsistent messages with ERR.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver asks the sender to stop and return unused allocation. By comparing the two records, the hosts can detect whether their accounts disagree and report a possible lost message.

sections.title: Make Inconsistencies Visible
sections.content:
The central argument is that an NCP should not silently change state to match an assumption about the other host. When a message conflicts with local state, Meyer proposes sending an ERR message and discarding the inconsistent message. The receiver of ERR should log it for human inspection and may take further steps to remove the inconsistency.

RFC 492 updates RFC 467, according to the unit metadata. It is a response and alternative proposal, not a complete replacement specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Meyer favors reporting a mismatch so people can see the error. He opposes quietly changing connection state in a way that may hide the cause.

references.text: Burchfiel, J. and R. Tomlinson, Network Request for Comments 467, BBN.
